newsitem.title: CANADA: Canadian miners slow to react to Zaire ultimatum.
newsitem.headline: Canadian miners slow to react to Zaire ultimatum.

text.p: Canadian mining companies that have been touched by rebellion in eastern Zaire have been slow to respond to a rebel ultimatum to discuss the future of their mining concessions.
Rebels controlling a large area of eastern Zaire said last week that foreign gold mining interests must come forward by January 3 or risk losing their assets in the region.

The rebels, called the Alliance of Democratic Forces for the Liberation of Congo-Zaire, are led by Laurent Kabila. Bent on the overthrow of Zaire's President Mobutu Sese Seko, they believe the region's rich mineral resources would enable them to finance their bid.
At least two Canadian companies have interests in the rebel-held area -- Toronto-based exploration company Banro Resource Corp and gold heavyweight Barrick Gold Corp.
However, a Banro spokesman said the company has no plans to negotiate with the rebels.
"We are in discussions with the Zaire Minister of Mining," said the spokesman, Cliff Jones.
Officials at Barrick Gold Corp, which has exploration properties in the Kilo-Moto area now under seige, said they were unaware of the ultimatum.

A Canadian businessman who claims to negotiate on behalf of significant North American mining interests in Zaire told Reuters on Thursday that he was trying to make contact with Kabila to determine the direction in which to take the companies' investments.
The businessman spoke on condition of anonymity.
On Thursday, the rebels seized the northeastern Zaire town of Bunia and nearby gold mines in a fierce battle with government forces which left hundreds dead, residents said.

The witnesses confirmed that the Kilo-Moto gold mining area 80 kilometres from Bunia was captured by the rebels. The Kimin gold mine, the largest in the area, was looted by Zairean troops. The mine is believed to be operated by a Belgian consortium.
